title: Money Without Qualities: Payment Dematerialization and the Erosion of Money’s Emotional and Symbolic Functions
content: Money is losing its material form. Research on payment digitalization has examined one consequence of this shift: digital payment weakens the pain of paying and increases spending. This article examines a broader one. The emotional and symbolic functions of money, its capacity to certify competence when earned, to express regard when given, to reassure when stored, and to mark boundaries when divided, depend on material properties that digital money lacks: tangibility, visibility, and ritual use. The article introduces the concept of symbolic attenuation to describe the weakening of these functions as the medium dematerializes. The concept addresses a specific gap. Existing research treats the meanings of money as properties of persons, measured as attitudes and dispositions, and treats the payment medium as psychologically neutral. Symbolic attenuation locates part of money's meaning in the medium itself, and therefore predicts that meanings change when the medium changes, holding persons constant. The distinction from reduced pain of paying is consequential, because the two accounts predict differently. Friction predicts overspending at the point of sale. Attenuation predicts effects far from it, in saving satisfaction, gift relations, children's financial socialization, and couple dynamics. The article derives testable propositions in each of these domains, shows that several existing findings on cash and cards fit attenuation better than friction, and outlines design principles for restoring symbolic weight to digital money.
